title: A man blamed me, and I blamed him for it
intro: Al-Tibrizi’s heading names Salih ibn Abd Allah ibn Salih al-Qurashi as the addressee. Abu Tammam begins by answering a critic, crosses difficult country and arrives at the door of a man who takes his praise and keeps him waiting. The swift, recurring rhyme comes to rest on an empty scabbard, the poet’s image for a gift that fails to reach its proper home.

translation: A man blamed me, and I blamed him for it.
In his ignorance he took me for a fool.
1.sharh: The critic finds his own conduct under examination. Three forms of the word for blame have already passed between the two men before the poet names the ignorance behind it.

translation: Nothing cheats a man like his own judgement.
Who ever gave you a brother flawless in every way?
2.sharh: A man can be worsted by his own reasoning. Al-Tibrizi recognises an old proverb in the second half. Even the friend you call a brother comes with faults.

translation: I have put on my youth. Let me wear it out,
with the judgement of a man steeped in the world’s troubles,
3.sharh: Youth is a new garment he means to use to the full. The judgement he claims for this apparently reckless choice is that of a man already immersed in the world’s disorder.

translation: one who knows his own camels’ song better than his critic,
whose life the hands of parting have scattered.
4.sharh: The camel-driver’s chant regulates the animals’ pace. He can conduct his own journey, and repeated separations have already taught him what a journey costs.

translation: Given strength and able to shoulder his load,
he flashes out like a sword drawn from its sheath.
5.sharh: Strength first appears as the ability to bear weight, then as the speed of a bare blade. The movement from burden to sudden action gives the portrait its spring.

translation: His ambition was born before he was.
Even the distinguished bow to his distinction.
6.sharh: Ambition seems to have been waiting for its owner to be born. The worth of the men who defer to him gives their deference particular weight.

translation: Like bitter sap, he is no sweet thing to taste,
unless you come to live under his shade.
7.sharh: The same plant offers an enemy its bitter taste and a dependant its shade. The two experiences belong to people standing in different relations to the man.

translation: He acquires wealth in plenty and gives it in plenty,
gathering it by ways forbidden and allowed.
8.sharh: The balanced clauses put acquisition beside open-handed giving. His resources come from every quarter, and the verse expressly includes both lawful and forbidden gains.

translation: He makes giving the readiest course for his wealth.
Many a land whose stopping place lies far away
9.sharh: Giving is the shortest way for money to leave his hand. Mid-verse the scene widens to a country with a distant halting place, and the traveller keeps us waiting for his verb.

translation: I crossed by night, each ride an arrow I let fly,
on a full-grown camel of choice breeding.
10.sharh: Distance is his target and the night’s travel his ammunition. Underneath that figure is an actual riding animal, mature and well bred on both sides.

translation: A man like me rode through such a night on such a beast.
And many a man, a king in his airs and station,
11.sharh: The three occurrences of “like” point in turn to rider, night and mount, as al-Tibrizi explains. A new encounter begins with a man who has all the outward standing of a king.

translation: a commoner in what he said and did,
I gave my praise in hope that he would give.
12.sharh: The grandee loses his royal standing the instant his behaviour enters the account. Praise has already changed hands, while the corresponding gift exists only in the poet’s hopes.

translation: He cut the rope of my hope off at the root,
after his delays had made a slave of me.
13.sharh: The promise kept its recipient bound to the giver. Cutting off hope now ends a long captivity in which the man’s only instrument was delay.

translation: Then he came pleading ignorance,
with a neck that honour had left unadorned.
14.sharh: Ignorance is a poor excuse after such a long postponement. The bare neck makes the loss of an opportunity for honour almost visible.

translation: He marvels at my amazement and at his own stinginess.
In earnest or in jest he looks at me
15.sharh: Even the miser professes amazement at his behaviour and at the poet’s response. Whatever the conversation’s mood, the look in his eyes stays the same.

translation: as a prisoner looks at the links of his chain,
as though I had come to strip him of office.
16.sharh: The poet has brought verse, yet the official looks at him as a captive looks at his irons. By the end, an ordinary appeal for a gift seems to threaten his whole position.

translation: You who stand alone in justice,
you clothed him in wealth. Give him no further respite.
17.sharh: The address turns upward to the giver of wealth. Al-Tibrizi’s editor takes the difficult final verb from granting someone time. The prayer asks that the favour cease to shelter such conduct.

translation: How wasted is a scabbard without its blade,
and poetry when it fails to find its people.
18.sharh: An empty scabbard still has its shape, but has lost its purpose. A poem placed in the wrong hands suffers the same fate. The reciter lets the whole comparison sound twice.

1.1.1.head: عاذِل
1.1.1.meaning: One who reproaches another for his conduct.

1.1.4.head: عَذل
1.1.4.meaning: His reproach. The poet turns the same word back on his critic three times. On the third occurrence the reciter’s consonant sounds close to d.

2.1.1-2.meaning: “Nothing short-changed”: nothing put him at a greater disadvantage.

2.2.4-5.head: بِأَخيكَ كُلِّه
2.2.4-5.meaning: “Your brother entire”: a friend whose every quality pleases you.

3.1.4.head: أَبلى
3.1.4.meaning: To wear a garment out through use.

3.2.6.head: خَبل
3.2.6.meaning: Disorder, damage, the troubles of life.

4.1.3.head: حُداء
4.1.3.meaning: Huda', the camel-driver’s chant that urges the herd along.

4.2.4.meaning: Separation and the distance it brings.

5.1.2.head: اِضطَلَعَ
5.1.2.meaning: To have the strength to shoulder a task. The two middle consonants run together in the recitation. Both diwans use the word for bearing a load.

5.2.1.head: اِنصَلَتَ
5.2.1.meaning: To flash forth, as a sword does when drawn.

7.1.1.head: الصّاب
7.1.1.meaning: Sab, a plant proverbial for its bitter sap.

9.1.2.head: النّائِل
9.1.2.meaning: A gift bestowed on a petitioner.

10.2.1.head: بازِل
10.2.1.meaning: Bazil, a camel whose mature canine teeth have come through.

10.2.2.head: مُقابَل
10.2.2.meaning: Well bred on both the sire’s and the dam’s side.

11.1.1-5.meaning: “My like rode in its like on its like”: rider, night and mount in that order.

12.1.1.head: سوقَة
12.1.1.meaning: An ordinary subject, a person outside the ruling class.

13.1.1.head: حَذَّ
13.1.1.meaning: To lop off or cut away completely.

13.2.5.head: مَطل
13.2.5.meaning: Putting off a claimant, keeping him waiting for what he is owed.

16.1.4.head: كَبل
16.1.4.meaning: A heavy fetter. The recording sounds close to kabrihi, with r. The commentary identifies the links of a prisoner’s shackle.

17.2.4.head: أَملى
17.2.4.meaning: To grant respite. The editor understands the manuscript wording in this sense.

18.1.5.head: نَصل
18.1.5.meaning: The metal blade within the scabbard.
